To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the effectiveness of a problem-solving market depends on the ability of the market to attract a broad range of participants; (b) a broad range of participation in the market depends on the openness of the problem-solving market, which is defined by the extent to which problem information is broadcasted; and (c) a broad range is defined in the context of the focal problem and the focal firm, and it depends on the extent of marginality of the problem and the firm.

the effectiveness of a science problem solving contest, characterized by open broadcast and blind review, depends on the marginality of solvers and that the provision of a winning submission was positively related to both technical and social marginalization.

(1) technical and social marginalities are important sources of problem-solving effectiveness; (2) the effectiveness of marginality increases with the level of difficulty of the problem; and (3) the effectiveness of female solvers is greater than that of male solvers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effectiveness of broadcast search for problem solving and the role of marginality in the process.
the effectiveness of broadcast search for solutions to scientific problems and the role of social and technical marginality in problem solving.
the effectiveness of open innovation and the role of marginality in the problem-solving process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the marginality of the solver is an important predictor for success, and the marginality of a solver increases with the distance between his or her field of expertise and the focal problem field.
marginality and problem-solving effectiveness are related, but not linear.
the marginality effect is not a simple one-way relationship, and the effect is not always beneficial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the marginality and problem-solving effectiveness is an important factor in the success of science problem solving contests.
marginality is a double edged sword in problem solving: it can be an impediment or a source of competitive advantage.
the more marginal you are the better you are in science problem-solving contests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
marginality, defined as a distance between a solver’s expertise and the focal problem, is positively related to problem solving performance, at least in science problem solving.

the effectiveness of open innovation is not only about the ability of a firm to access new sources of knowledge, but also about the ability to access new perspectives and heuristically different approaches to solving internal problems.
the marginality of problem solvers can be an asset in solving complex problems.
